name: Cucumber extract

lead: Cucumber extract is made from the fruit or seeds of the cucumber plant and appears in gels, toners and eye products as a cooling, soothing ingredient.
Its reputation rests largely on the fruit being mostly water and on the familiar image of cucumber slices on the eyes. Published research on skin outcomes is essentially absent.

paras: Manufacturers describe it as hydrating and soothing. No studies in the sources reviewed have measured a specific mechanism on human skin.

Oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies of a standardized extract exist, but they concern ingestion. Topical risks are those of any plant-based cosmetic, mainly individual irritation or allergy to the finished product.

lead: Cucumber extract is a preparation made from the fruit, and sometimes the seeds, of Cucumis sativus, an annual vine of the gourd family that has been cultivated for at least 3,000 years [1]. In skincare it is listed as a cooling, soothing botanical, and it is usually included in cleansers, toners, gels and eye products for its fresh-feel and mild, hydrating character rather than as an active ingredient.

The raw fruit is about 95 percent water, which is the basis of its reputation as a hydrating, cooling ingredient [1]. Published research on "cucumber extract" is sparse and mixed in topic: many indexed papers actually concern sea cucumbers, which are unrelated marine animals, and several others use cucumber extract as a laboratory reagent rather than as a skincare product [2][3].

For appearance use, no published human trial in the sources reviewed has shown that cucumber extract improves skin. A standardized cucumber extract has been assessed in oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies [4], and a small trial of cucumber seed extract for sun-induced redness is registered [5].
infobox: At least 3,000 years, domesticated in India [1]

paras: Cucumber is botanically a pepo, a type of berry, though it is treated as a vegetable in cooking. Slicing, pickling and seedless types are the main groups [1]. The raw fruit with peel is mostly water with small amounts of carbohydrate and protein, and polyphenol content is higher in unpeeled fruit [1]. Cucurbitacins give the rind a slightly bitter taste [1].

Cosmetic extracts may be made from the juice, the fruit pulp or the seeds. A branded standardized cucumber extract, sold for use as a nutraceutical ingredient, has been the subject of published safety work [4].

Cucumber slices on the eyes are a long-standing popular beauty image, and the extract appears in products marketed to soothe, cool or refresh skin. Its role in these products is generally described by manufacturers as soothing and hydrating; the sources reviewed contain no controlled study of cucumber extract on puffiness, dark circles, redness or other appearance outcomes.
In looksmaxxing discussion it appears mainly as a minor ingredient in basic skincare routines rather than as a subject of dedicated threads.

A standardized cucumber extract was examined in repeat-dose oral toxicity and mutagenicity studies, which are the type of work used to support safety of an ingredient [4]. These studies concern ingestion and do not directly address topical use on skin. As with other plant extracts, individual allergic or irritant reactions to fragrance or preservative components in finished products are possible.

No published clinical trial in the sources reviewed has tested cucumber extract for a cosmetic outcome. Registered trials include a trial of cucumber seed extract versus placebo for sun-induced skin redness (minimal erythema dose) in 29 adults with Fitzpatrick skin types III to V, which is listed as completed [5], and trials of cucumber extract or supplement for joint pain and osteoarthritis [6][7]. Results of these registrations are not summarized in the sources reviewed. Studies of sea cucumber extracts, including several in cancer models and one in a rat liver injury model, concern a different organism and are not evidence about the garden cucumber [2][3].
